questions.q: What does a validation-only deployment actually do?
options: It skips Apex tests entirely to save time
It runs every deploy check -- compiling, testing, checking coverage -- against the target org without making any change permanent
It deletes metadata from the target org
It only checks spelling in component names
questions.explain: Validation proves a deployment would succeed by running the real checks, but without committing the change -- so a failure costs you none of the actual deployment risk.

questions.q: How long is a validation job ID from sf project deploy validate usable before it expires?
options: 24 hours
30 days
It never expires
10 days
questions.explain: A validation job ID is valid for 10 days from when the validation started, after which it can no longer be quick-deployed.

questions.q: What does sf project deploy quick --job-id do differently from a normal sf project deploy start?
options: It deploys the already-validated metadata without re-running Apex tests, since that risk was already retired by validation
It re-runs every Apex test a second time for extra safety
It only works on sandboxes
It requires a brand new manifest file
questions.explain: Quick deploy skips re-running tests because the referenced validation job already proved the deployment and its tests would pass.

questions.q: Per Salesforce's own guidance, what should you use instead of sf project deploy validate when checking a deployment against a sandbox?
options: sf package version create
sf apex run test with no other flags
sf project deploy start with the --dry-run flag
There is no equivalent check available for sandboxes
questions.explain: deploy validate / deploy quick is intended for production; for sandboxes, --dry-run on the regular deploy start command serves the same 'check without committing' purpose.

questions.q: Why does a pipeline benefit from separating 'validate' from 'quick deploy' as two distinct steps?
options: It cleanly separates proving a change is safe from the deliberate act of actually releasing it, mirroring Continuous Delivery's human-approved release gate
Because Salesforce requires exactly 10 days between the two steps
Because validation and quick deploy must always run on different orgs
There is no benefit, it's purely a historical CLI quirk
questions.explain: Splitting verification from release lets a team automate the proof step while keeping a deliberate, separate action for the actual release -- the same split Continuous Delivery draws generally.
